Isolation Precautions & PPE

Isolation precautions, types of transmission-based precautions and correct PPE use.

🎯 After this chapter you can

  • Describe standard and transmission-based precautions
  • List contact, droplet and airborne precautions
  • Demonstrate correct PPE donning and doffing order

In simple words

Isolation precautions stop germs spreading from infectious patients to others. Standard precautions apply to every patient. Transmission-based precautions (contact, droplet, airborne) are added for specific infections.

PPE (gloves, mask, gown, goggles) protects the nurse. The order of putting on and taking off matters for safety.

Standard precautions (every patient)

  • Hand hygiene before and after contact.
  • Gloves when touching blood, body fluids, mucous membranes.
  • Mask and eye protection if splashes are likely.
  • Gown if clothing may be soiled.
  • Safe sharps handling and disposal.

Transmission-based precautions

Type Spread by Example Key measure
Contact Touch MRSA, C. difficile Gown + gloves for room entry
Droplet Large droplets (cough, talk) Influenza, pertussis Mask within 1 metre
Airborne Small particles stay in air TB, chickenpox, measles N95 respirator, negative pressure room

PPE order

Donning: gown → mask → goggles → gloves. Doffing: gloves → goggles → gown → mask (mask last, outside room). Perform hand hygiene between steps and at the end.

🔴 Mask comes off last

Remove the mask last, outside the room. It has been closest to your face and may be contaminated.

Where the nurse uses this

  • Every patient — standard precautions: hand hygiene, gloves for body fluids.
  • Infectious patient — follow the isolation sign (contact, droplet or airborne).
  • PPE — put on before entering, remove correctly before leaving.
  • Sharps — never recap needles; use puncture-proof containers.
  • Patient placement — airborne infections need negative pressure rooms.

🔴 Most important for exams

  1. Standard precautions apply to every patient.
  2. Contact precautions: gown + gloves for room entry (MRSA, C. difficile).
  3. Droplet precautions: mask within 1 metre (influenza, pertussis).
  4. Airborne precautions: N95 respirator + negative pressure room (TB, chickenpox, measles).
  5. PPE donning: gown → mask → goggles → gloves.
  6. PPE doffing: gloves → goggles → gown → mask (mask last, outside room).

⭐ Important for exams

  1. Hand hygiene before and after every patient contact.
  2. Never recap needles; use sharps containers.
  3. Goggles protect eyes from splashes.
  4. Perform hand hygiene between PPE removal steps and at the end.

📌 Memory trick

PPE doffing: “G-G-G-M” — Gloves, Goggles, Gown, Mask (last).

60-second revision

  • Standard precautions = every patient.
  • Contact = gown + gloves; Droplet = mask within 1m; Airborne = N95 + negative room.
  • Donning: gown → mask → goggles → gloves.
  • Doffing: gloves → goggles → gown → mask (last, outside room).
  • Hand hygiene between steps and at end.

Test yourself

TB requires:

Answer: C. TB spreads by small airborne particles — needs N95 respirator and negative pressure room.

PPE should be removed in this order:

Answer: B. Remove gloves first (most contaminated), mask last and outside the room.

Droplet precautions need a mask within:

Answer: A. Droplets travel short distances — mask within about 1 metre of the patient.

Standard precautions apply to:

Answer: B. Standard precautions apply to every patient, every time.

C. difficile requires:

Answer: B. C. difficile spreads by contact and spores — needs contact precautions (gown + gloves) and soap-and-water hand hygiene.
